headline: Season choice depends on whether you prioritize migrants or resident breeding displays
summary: Green season (November-April) offers Palearctic migrants in fresh plumage, resident birds in breeding dress, and higher overall species counts. Dry season (June-October) provides better visibility in sparse vegetation, easier access to waterholes where birds concentrate, and more comfortable birding conditions. Neither season is definitively better - the decision hinges on your target species list and tolerance for challenging field conditions.

assumptions.text: Palearctic migrants are present from November through March in most East African locations.
Resident species display breeding plumage and behavior during early rains (November-December).
Dense green season vegetation reduces visibility but increases overall bird activity.

gains: Green season: 30-40% higher species counts with migrants present
Green season: Breeding displays, nest building, courtship behavior
Dry season: Easier bird photography with sparse backgrounds
Dry season: Waterhole concentration makes species predictable
losses: Green season: Muddy roads may limit access to forest habitats
Green season: Skulking behavior in dense vegetation frustrates identification
Dry season: Miss all Palearctic migrants and inter-African migrants
Dry season: Resident species in dull non-breeding plumage

change_conditions: If your target list includes specific Palearctic migrants (e.g., warblers, raptors), green season is mandatory.
If combining birding with Big Five game viewing as primary goal, dry season optimizes both.
If photography is the priority, dry season backgrounds and waterhole setups produce cleaner images.
If visiting Uganda or Rwanda for forest endemics, seasonality matters less than for savannah birding.
